# The Scale Ladder

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: There is no single right enterprise brain; the right one depends on the organisation's stage. Each size, from two people to ten thousand, has a different problem for the decision record to solve: false shared memory, the first stranger, meaning, delegation, governance and density. This hub sets out the whole ladder, what to build at each rung, the risk at each, and the five invariants that hold at every size.

There is no single right enterprise brain. There is a right one for two people, a different one for fifty, and a very different one for 10,000. What changes as an organisation grows is not whether it needs a record of its judgment, but which problem that record has to solve: false shared memory at two people, the first stranger at ten, meaning at fifty, delegation at two hundred, governance at a thousand and density at ten thousand. The mistake at every size is building the brain of the wrong stage. The rule is to build for the next rung, not two rungs up.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Most writing about enterprise brains assumes a large, regulated organisation with platform teams, data stewards and a compliance function. Most organisations are not that, and the ones that are did not start that way. Every 10,000-person firm was once two people in a room, deciding things and remembering why, until one day they did not.

The SBA Office of Advocacy's 2026 profile, built on 2022 Census data, counts about 6.4 million small employer firms and 21,041 large businesses with 500 or more employees. Small businesses employ 45.9% of private-sector workers. Advice written for a 10,000-person firm does real harm when applied at fifty.

This piece is the hub of an eight-part series, with a page for each rung and a closing piece on the five invariants. Our companion piece [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) covers which layers to rent and which to own at each size, and [*Building the commercial system at every size*](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/) applies the same ladder to sales, marketing and pricing.

## Why one design cannot fit every size

The first reason is arithmetic. Fred Brooks observed in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975) that adding people to a late software project makes it later, partly because communication paths grow as n(n-1)/2. The formula describes possible channels, not actual conversations, but it shows why informal memory stops working.

| Headcount | Possible pairwise channels | What that means for memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 1 | Two memories of every decision, and no third party to settle disputes |
| 10 | 45 | Founders can still answer every question, but it becomes their main job |
| 50 | 1,225 | Teams form, and each develops its own vocabulary |
| 200 | 19,900 | Most decisions are made by people the founders never talk to |
| 1,000 | 499,500 | Functions exist whose job is to question other functions' decisions |
| 10,000 | 49,995,000 | Enough repeated decisions to learn from, and too many records to unify |

The organisational research points the same way. J. Richard Hackman, interviewed in *Harvard Business Review* in 2009, said the number of links a team must manage rises "at an accelerating, almost exponential rate" as it grows, and gave his rule of thumb for team size as "no double digits". An organisation is not a team, but it is made of them, and the links between teams grow the same way.

Research on social group sizes suggests the breaks come in steps rather than smoothly. Zhou, Sornette, Hill and Dunbar's analysis, published by the Royal Society in 2005, found human group sizes cluster in a hierarchy with a scaling ratio close to three. That pattern, not any single number, is why a ladder with distinct rungs is a better model than a smooth curve.

The second reason is that scrutiny and tooling change with size too. The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found AI use rising among firms with 20 or more employees in the six months to May 2026, reaching 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of those with 250 or more. Fewer than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using it. Regulation bites at size thresholds as well, as the governance rung below shows.

## Six rungs, six problems

**Two people: false shared memory.** Two founders remember the same decision differently, and neither is lying. Memory favours the version that fits each person's own view. Ross and Sicoly's classic 1979 study, as summarised by Caruso, Epley and Bazerman in 2006, found that when spouses each estimated their own share of household tasks, including important decisions, the estimates summed to more than 100%. The record's job is to be the one version both founders wrote at the time. See [*Two people: the founders' ledger*](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/).

**Ten people: the first stranger.** New hires do not share the founders' history, and every "why do we..." question routes to a founder. McKinsey Global Institute estimated in 2012 that interaction workers spend nearly 20% of their time looking for internal information or tracking down colleagues who can help. At ten people, the colleague is usually a founder. See [*Ten people: the first stranger*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/).

**Fifty people: meaning.** Teams form, and the same words start to mean different things in different rooms. "Customer" means a signed contract to finance and anyone in a trial to marketing. At the same time, each team adopts its own AI tools: Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index found 78% of AI users were bringing their own tools to work. Each tool keeps its own memory. See [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/).

**Two hundred people: delegation.** Founders no longer make most decisions; managers do, and the reasoning has to travel without them. Inconsistency becomes measurable. In a noise audit described by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues, executives at an insurer expected about a 10% difference between underwriters' quotes on the same case; the typical difference was 55%. See [*Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author*](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/).

**One thousand people: governance.** Auditors, regulators, risk functions and security teams arrive, and "we decided it in a meeting" stops being an acceptable record. In the EU, the Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force from 18 March 2026, sets the scope of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive at more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450 million of turnover. See [*One thousand people: governance arrives*](https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/).

**Ten thousand people: density.** There is finally enough volume in enough decision classes for a system to learn, and the challenge is federation: one organisation, many records. The same Omnibus I Directive puts the due diligence directive's scope at more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5 billion of turnover. See [*Ten thousand people: density, and the case for federation*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-thousand-people-density-and-the-case-for-federation/).

> What changes as an organisation grows is not whether it needs a judgment record. It is which problem the record has to solve.

## The ladder in one table

The table summarises each rung. The headcounts are approximate; the problems are the diagnosis.

| Rung | Approximate headcount | What breaks | What the record must do | What to build | The risk at this rung |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founders | 2 | Shared memory: two honest versions of each decision | Be the single version both wrote at the time | One append-only ledger, a 30-minute weekly review, transcription with consent | Building a knowledge base instead of the habit |
| First stranger | About 10 | Context: newcomers cannot see why anything is done | Answer "why do we do it this way?" without a founder | A ledger strangers can read, "why we do it" pages, first definitions, onboarding through the record | A topic wiki that decays within weeks |
| Meaning | About 50 | Vocabulary: teams define the same words differently | Hold one current definition of each term, and one home for records | A glossary of 20 to 30 terms with owners, written decision rights, a conflicts list | Every team's AI tool keeping its own memory |
| Delegation | About 200 | Precedent: managers inherit decisions from people who have left | Let reasoning travel without its author | Formal decision classes, a precedent slot, handover packs, first calibration | Compliance theatre: long templates filled to satisfy a process |
| Governance | About 1,000 | Defensibility: outsiders ask how decisions were made | Let any AI-assisted decision be reconstructed end to end | A trace specification, an evidenced review gate, agent registration, retention rules | A platform team owning a record that is technically sound and commercially empty |
| Density | About 10,000 | Unity: one model of everything stalls | Let many records learn, and map between them | Central invariants and export format, local records, a definitions map | A single enterprise ontology that takes years and is used by nobody |

Each rung has a characteristic failure, and each is a good idea at the wrong size. The ten-person wiki is a large firm's tool used too early. The single enterprise ontology is a small firm's instinct, one definition of everything, applied at a size it cannot survive.

## Five things that change with size

**Decision volume per class.** Low and heterogeneous when small; high and repetitive when large. Two founders make a few dozen significant decisions in their first year, nearly all different. A large lender or insurer can make thousands of comparable calls a week. Only the second can be learned from, which is why our piece [*Below the volume floor*](https://lowob.com/research/below-the-volume-floor/) argues against expecting a small firm's record to train anything.

**Distance between decider and consequence.** Zero at two people; several layers at 10,000. The further a decision travels, the more its reason must be written down.

**Turnover of context.** Rare at first; constant later, through hiring, rotation and departures. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported median tenure with the current employer of 4.1 years in January 2026, and 3.9 years in the private sector. In a firm of several hundred, many of the people who set a precedent will have gone before it is questioned.

**External scrutiny.** Investors at first; then customers, auditors and regulators. The thresholds are explicit. In US banking, SR 26-2, issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC, replaced SR 11-7 and is expected to be most relevant to banks with more than $30 billion of assets. In the EU, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved the AI Act's Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027.

**Who maintains the record.** Founders; then everyone; then a function; then a platform. Each change of maintainer is a moment when the record can lose its purpose.

| Variable | 2 people | 50 people | 1,000 people | 10,000 people |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decision volume per class | A handful, all different | Dozens, some recurring | Hundreds, classed | Thousands, comparable |
| Decider to consequence | Same person | One team away | Several layers | Divisions apart |
| Context turnover | Rare | Each new hire | Monthly | Constant |
| External scrutiny | Investors | Investors, early customers | Auditors, regulators, large customers | All of these, in several jurisdictions |
| Record maintained by | Founders | Everyone, with owners for terms | Business functions, with platform standards | Functions locally, invariants centrally |

## Build for the next rung, not two rungs up

The practical rule is to build the layer the next stage will break, not the one the stage after that. A ten-person company that builds a governed ontology is spending money on a problem it does not have, and the ontology will be wrong by the time it matters. A 1,000-person company still running decisions through a founders' document is about to discover the problem it skipped.

The two errors are not symmetrical. Over-building early costs time and money, and the structure goes stale before it is needed. Under-building late costs more, because the reasons behind past decisions cannot be recovered once their authors have left. Michael Nygard's 2011 case for architecture decision records describes the result: a newcomer facing an unexplained decision can only blindly accept it or blindly change it. Neither is safe.

The rungs are approximate, and the evidence on group size supports reading them loosely. Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind's 2021 re-analysis of the data behind "Dunbar's number" found estimates of maximum human group size so uncertain that the 95% interval for their main model ran from about 4 to 292. A fixed cognitive limit on group size, they concluded, cannot be derived in this way. Headcount is a proxy for the problem, not the problem itself.

A regulated fintech may hit the governance rung at 80 people, when a bank partner or regulator asks how a credit decision was made. A research lab may stay at the meaning rung for years. A firm that grows by acquisition can meet federation at 2,000 people, because it has inherited several records at once. Read the problem, not the headcount.

| Symptom | Rung it signals | First thing to build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The founders describe last month's big decision differently | Founders | An append-only ledger |
| Founders answer more questions each week as hiring continues | First stranger | Ledger entries a stranger can read |
| Two dashboards disagree in a board meeting | Meaning | A glossary with owners |
| Similar cases get different answers from different managers | Delegation | Decision classes and a precedent slot |
| A customer security review asks who approved an AI action | Governance | A trace specification |
| A central data model has been "nearly finished" for two years | Density | Central invariants and a definitions map |

**In practice:** identify the current rung by its problem. Name the problem of the next rung, and build only what solves that. Revisit the diagnosis every time headcount roughly doubles, or when an event such as an acquisition, a regulator or a large customer changes the problem without changing the headcount.

## The five invariants underneath

Almost everything about the record changes with size: the tools, the owners, the governance, the automation, whether it can learn. Five things do not. They are what make the record a record of judgment rather than a pile of content, and our closing piece, [*Five invariants, from two people to ten thousand*](https://lowob.com/research/five-invariants-from-two-people-to-ten-thousand/), sets them out in full.

| Invariant | At two people | At ten thousand people |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decisions carry a reason and a falsifier | A line in a shared document | A required field in every decision workflow |
| Sources are kept; summaries are views | A link to the call note or email | Evidence stored with timestamp and origin |
| Views are superseded, never overwritten | A new entry that names the old one | Version history enforced by the platform |
| Outcomes are written back | A weekly check of falsifier dates | Calibration reports by decision class |
| The organisation owns the record | A document both founders can export | An export format every tool must support |

The invariants cost almost nothing at two people and are the hardest thing to retrofit at ten thousand. Each rung adds volume, automation, governance or federation on top of them. None of these substitutes for the invariants, and all of them amplify whatever the invariants are, good or bad. Our explainer [*What is a decision record?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) covers the basic fields.

## What would prove this wrong

The ladder is a claim about sequencing, and it can be tested. It would be wrong if organisations that build the full large-scale stack early gained from it at every stage, without excess cost or rework. Then the ladder is a false economy, and firms should build the 10,000-person brain at fifty.

It would also be weakened if the problems did not arrive in roughly this order. If most firms met governance before meaning, the ladder would need reordering. Regulated sectors are the clearest exception we know of.

## lowob takeaways

- **Diagnose by problem, not headcount.** Memory, strangers, meaning, delegation, governance and density arrive roughly in that order, at sizes that vary by sector.
- **Build for the next rung.** Solve the problem you are about to meet, not one two rungs away.
- **Expect each rung's characteristic failure.** The wiki at ten, tool sprawl at fifty, compliance theatre at two hundred, platform ownership at a thousand, the single ontology at ten thousand.
- **Hold the five invariants from day one.** They are cheap at two people and nearly impossible to retrofit at scale.
- **Revisit at each doubling.** Or sooner, when an acquisition, regulator or large customer changes the problem.

## Common questions

### How should a company's knowledge system change as it grows?

The record has to solve a different problem at each stage: false shared memory at two people, the first stranger at about ten, meaning at fifty, delegation at two hundred, governance at a thousand, then density and federation at ten thousand. Build only for the next stage.

### What breaks first when a startup grows?

Shared memory, then context. Two founders remember decisions differently, and from the first hires onward every "why do we do this?" question routes to a founder unless the reasons are written down.

### Should a small startup build a knowledge graph or ontology?

No. A ten-person company that builds one is spending on a problem it does not have, and the structure will be wrong by the time it matters. A shared, append-only decision ledger does more at that size.

### Is Dunbar's number a reliable guide to when a company needs more structure?

Only loosely. Group sizes appear to cluster in steps, but a 2021 re-analysis found the evidence too uncertain to support a fixed limit near 150. Diagnose by symptoms, such as conflicting definitions or inconsistent decisions, not by a headcount threshold.
